## Guided Tutorial 5.2: Bringing Dates and Groups onto the Invoice Lines

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will use lookups to bring the attributes the controller's question needs onto each invoice line: the invoice date and period from the invoice, the order date from the sales order, and the item group and product type from the item. You will check that every lookup found its match, reconcile the Furniture revenue by quarter to the totals you reconciled in the Part I case, and find the promotion lines that were invoiced after the promotion ended.

**Prerequisites.** You need the analysis workbook from Tutorial 5.1, with the ProductType column on the Item Table and the Period column on the SalesInvoice Table.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Import the sales orders.** The order date lives in the SalesOrder Table, which the workbook does not have yet. Import it as you imported the other Tables in Chapter 4.

a. Choose **Data > Get Data > From File > From Excel Workbook**, select CharlesRiver.xlsx, and select the **T9_SalesOrder** Table in the **Navigator**. Click **Transform Data**.
b. Rename the query `SalesOrder`, and use **Home > Choose Columns** to keep SalesOrderID, OrderNumber, OrderDate, CustomerID, and Status.
c. Set the OrderDate column's data type to **Date** if it shows a time.
d. Choose **Home > Close & Load**, and rename the new worksheet `SalesOrder`.

**Step 2. Bring the invoice date and period onto each line.** Go to the **SalesInvoiceLine** worksheet and add the new columns to the right of DiscountAmount, the last calculated column you added in Chapter 4.

a. Add a column `InvoiceDate` with this formula, and format the column as a date:

   ```
   =XLOOKUP([@SalesInvoiceID],SalesInvoice[SalesInvoiceID],SalesInvoice[InvoiceDate],"No match")
   ```

b. Add a column `Period` with the same formula, returning `SalesInvoice[Period]` instead of `SalesInvoice[InvoiceDate]`.

**Step 3. Follow the key from the invoice to the order.** The order date is two keys away: the line leads to its invoice, and the invoice leads to its order.

a. Add a column `SalesOrderID` that returns `SalesInvoice[SalesOrderID]` with the same lookup as in Step 2.
b. Add a column `OrderDate` with this formula, and format it as a date:

   ```
   =XLOOKUP([@SalesOrderID],SalesOrder[SalesOrderID],SalesOrder[OrderDate],"No match")
   ```

**Step 4. Bring the item group and product type onto each line.**

a. Add a column `ItemGroup` with this formula:

   ```
   =XLOOKUP([@ItemID],Item[ItemID],Item[ItemGroup],"No match")
   ```

b. Add a column `ProductType` with the same formula, returning `Item[ProductType]`.

**Step 5. Check that every lookup found its match.** A lookup that fails returns "No match", so counting that value tests every lookup.

a. On the **Analysis** worksheet, type `Lookups not matched` in A41.
b. The six new columns sit side by side, so one COUNTIF can search them all. In B41, enter this formula, which uses a structured reference to the range of columns from InvoiceDate to ProductType:

   ```
   =COUNTIF(SalesInvoiceLine[[InvoiceDate]:[ProductType]],"No match")
   ```

B41 should show zero. Every invoice line found its invoice, every invoice found its order, and every item sold is among the items you kept in Chapter 4, so the lookups are complete.

**Step 6. Reconcile the Furniture revenue by quarter.** The lines now carry a period and an item group, so their revenue can be summed by both.

a. On the **Analysis** worksheet, type `Furniture revenue by quarter` in A43, and type the labels `2026-Q1`, `2026-Q2`, `2026-Q3`, and `2026-Q4` in B44 through E44.
b. In B45, enter this formula, then copy B45 and paste it into C45:E45 (copy and paste rather than drag, as Chapter 4 explained):

   ```
   =SUMIFS(SalesInvoiceLine[LineTotal],SalesInvoiceLine[ItemGroup],"Furniture",SalesInvoiceLine[Period],B$44)
   ```

c. Compare the third and fourth quarters with the Furniture revenue you reconciled to the ledger in the Part I case.

The totals should agree to the cent. That agreement is evidence that the lookups assigned every Furniture line to the right group and the right quarter.

**Step 7. Find the promotion lines invoiced after the promotion ended.**

a. On the **SalesInvoiceLine** worksheet, use the PromotionID slicer from Chapter 4 to show promotion 8, the Furniture Seasonal Promotion.
b. Open the filter list on the InvoiceDate column and choose **Date Filters > After**, and enter 2026-10-31, the promotion's end date.
c. Read the status bar, and look at the OrderDate column of the lines in view.
d. On the **Analysis** worksheet, record the count with this formula in B47, with the label `Promotion 8 lines invoiced after its end date` in A47:

   ```
   =COUNTIFS(SalesInvoiceLine[PromotionID],8,SalesInvoiceLine[InvoiceDate],">"&DATE(2026,10,31))
   ```

e. Clear the filters.

More than a hundred promotion lines were invoiced in November and December, after the promotion ended, and every one of them comes from an order placed while the promotion was running. The promotional price was set when the order was placed, but the revenue was recorded when the order was invoiced. @fig-05-05 shows some of these lines.

![Invoice Lines with Their Looked-Up Dates and Groups.](/visuals/svg/fig-05-05-invoice-line-lookups.svg){#fig-05-05 fig-alt="A mock of the SalesInvoiceLine Table with the lookup columns added in this tutorial: InvoiceDate, Period, SalesOrderID, OrderDate, ItemGroup, and ProductType, next to the line's ID, promotion, and line total. The rows shown are Furniture lines of the Furniture Seasonal Promotion invoiced in December 2026, after the promotion's end date, whose orders were placed in September and October 2026. The InvoiceDate and OrderDate columns are outlined, and the formula bar shows the XLOOKUP formula for InvoiceDate."}

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the SalesInvoiceLine Table has six new lookup columns, and none of them contains "No match";
- the Furniture revenue for 2026-Q3 and 2026-Q4 agrees with the Part I case;
- you have counted the promotion 8 lines invoiced after the promotion's end date.

The last finding changes how the controller's question should be read. The promotion's effect on the fourth quarter depends on when its orders were invoiced, not only on its effective dates, so a quarter-by-quarter analysis must use the invoice date for revenue and keep the order date in view to explain it.
